reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Most lesions occur at the carotid bifurcation and proximal internal carotid artery, where atherosclerotic plaque and turbulence predispose to thromboembolism
Symptomatic disease typically presents as ipsilateral transient ischaemic attack, amaurosis fugax, or hemispheric stroke rather than global symptoms
A cervical bruit is neither sensitive nor specific and its absence does not exclude significant stenosis
Duplex ultrasound is the usual first-line imaging, with CT or MR angiography used to confirm the degree of narrowing and assess the aortic arch and intracranial circulation
Risk stratification hinges on whether the lesion is symptomatic and on the percentage stenosis, as benefit from intervention is greatest in recently symptomatic high-grade lesions
Best medical therapy with antiplatelet agents, lipid lowering, blood pressure control, and smoking cessation is fundamental for all patients regardless of intervention
Carotid endarterectomy and carotid artery stenting are the two revascularisation options, with choice guided by anatomy, age, comorbidity, and operative risk
Intervention for symptomatic disease is most effective when performed early after the index neurological event
reference.pathophysiology: Carotid artery stenosis is usually caused by atherosclerotic plaque forming at the carotid bifurcation, a site of low and oscillating wall shear stress. Progressive plaque growth narrows the lumen, but the dominant mechanism of stroke is artery-to-artery thromboembolism from an unstable, ulcerated, or haemorrhagic plaque rather than simple flow limitation. Plaque rupture exposes thrombogenic material, generating platelet-fibrin and cholesterol emboli that lodge in the ophthalmic or middle cerebral territory. In severe stenosis or occlusion, cerebral perfusion may also become haemodynamically compromised, particularly when collateral supply through the circle of Willis is inadequate.
additionalDifferentials: Cardioembolic stroke from atrial fibrillation or structural heart disease
Fibromuscular dysplasia of the carotid artery
additionalInvestigations: Carotid duplex ultrasound to estimate stenosis severity and plaque characteristics
CT angiography or MR angiography to confirm stenosis and evaluate arch and intracranial vessels
Brain imaging (CT or MRI) to identify infarction in symptomatic patients
Cardiac evaluation including ECG and echocardiography to exclude a cardioembolic source
Vascular risk-factor profiling including lipids and glucose
redFlags: Recent transient ischaemic attack, amaurosis fugax, or stroke with high-grade ipsilateral stenosis, indicating high early stroke risk and need for urgent assessment
Crescendo TIAs or stroke-in-evolution suggesting an unstable plaque
Acute focal neurological deficit requiring emergency stroke pathway activation
Contralateral occlusion or near-occlusion increasing haemodynamic vulnerability
reference.prognosis: Recently symptomatic high-grade stenosis carries a substantial short-term risk of recurrent stroke that is markedly reduced by timely revascularisation combined with medical therapy. Asymptomatic disease has a lower annual stroke risk, and modern medical therapy has narrowed the margin of benefit from intervention.
pitfalls: Relying on a bruit or its absence to gauge stenosis severity
Delaying revascularisation in recently symptomatic patients, forfeiting the greatest window of benefit
Overestimating benefit of intervention in asymptomatic patients with limited life expectancy
Neglecting global vascular risk-factor modification while focusing only on the carotid lesion
management: Institute best medical therapy for all patients: antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, blood-pressure control, glycaemic control and smoking cessation
Offer carotid endarterectomy, or stenting in selected patients, promptly for recently symptomatic high-grade stenosis
Treat acute transient ischaemic attack or stroke and expedite revascularisation within the window of greatest benefit
Weigh intervention more cautiously in asymptomatic disease, where modern medical therapy has narrowed the margin of benefit
Monitor with surveillance carotid duplex ultrasound and exclude a cardioembolic source
Coordinate vascular surgery, neurology and stroke-prevention care
